item.title: C Programming: Choosing Between signal() and sigaction() for Signal Handling
item.description:
“C Programming: Choosing Between signal() and sigaction() for Signal Handling”

Reliability and Semantics Comparison: signal() Versus sigaction()

Why is sigaction() generally recommended over signal() for establishing signal handlers?

The signal() interface carries significant baggage due to its historical ambiguity and system-dependent behavior. While it is defined in the C standard, its implementation varies widely across operating systems, leading to portability concerns.

Key issues with signal() include:

  1. Handler Reinstallation: By default, signal() often resets the signal disposition back to SIG_DFL (default behavior) after the handler executes for nearly all signals. This necessitates that the handler immediately re-installs itself as its first action. If a second instance of the same signal arrives before reinstallation, the default, often fatal, action occurs, creating a window of vulnerability.
  2. Signal Blocking: signal() typically does not reliably block other signals from arriving while the current handler is active.
  3. System Variance: The Open Group explicitly states that the semantics of using signal() to establish a handler vary across UNIX versions, and POSIX permits this variation.

In contrast, sigaction() offers finer, explicit control over signal invocation semantics and avoids the race conditions associated with automatic handler resetting.

item.title: Exploring Ruby Methods for External Shell Command Execution
item.description:
“Exploring Ruby Methods for External Shell Command Execution”

When developing Ruby applications, interacting with the operating system’s shell is a common requirement for automation, running system utilities, or executing external scripts. Ruby provides several mechanisms for this purpose, each with distinct characteristics regarding output capture, process replacement, and error handling. A critical initial consideration is that Ruby often invokes /bin/sh, not necessarily bash, meaning shell syntax compatibility across systems needs verification.

item.title: Register Preservation Across Function Calls in C: A Deep Dive
item.description:
“Register Preservation Across Function Calls in C: A Deep Dive”

When writing code in C, particularly when interacting with low-level operations or optimizing performance, understanding how functions manage registers is crucial. This topic delves into the nuances of register preservation across function calls, focusing on the roles of callee-saved and scratch registers, and how compilers like GCC adhere to (or deviate from) the established Application Binary Interface (ABI).

What are Callee-Saved and Scratch Registers?

In the context of function calls, registers are temporary storage locations within the CPU. To ensure that functions can call each other without corrupting critical data, a convention is established for how registers should be treated.

item.title: How to Invoke System Calls: A Deep Dive into x86 Assembly Calling Conventions
item.description:
“How to Invoke System Calls: A Deep Dive into x86 Assembly Calling Conventions”

System calls are the fundamental interface between user-space programs and the operating system kernel. Understanding how these calls are made, particularly at the assembly level, is crucial for low-level programming, reverse engineering, and performance optimization. This post delves into the intricacies of system call and function calling conventions on x86-32 and x86-64 architectures, providing detailed explanations and practical examples.

item.title: Diagnosing Duplicate Output After fork() in C: Buffering & Flushing Explained
item.description:
“Diagnosing Duplicate Output After fork() in C: Buffering & Flushing Explained”

When working with process creation using fork() in C, a common pitfall is observing unexpected duplicate output, especially when standard output (stdout) is involved. This behavior stems from how stdout buffering mechanisms interact with the process duplication. Let’s delve into why this happens and how to manage it effectively.

The Core Issue: Standard Output Buffering

Standard output in C is typically buffered. This means that data written to stdout isn’t immediately sent to the terminal or destination. Instead, it’s held in an internal buffer until certain conditions are met, such as the buffer becoming full, a newline character being encountered (for line-buffered output), or an explicit flush operation.

item.title: Safe C Signal Handler Functions: Avoiding printf Pitfalls
item.description:
“Safe C Signal Handler Functions: Avoiding printf Pitfalls”

When crafting signal handlers in C, a critical consideration is which standard library functions can be safely called. The core issue arises from potential reentrancy problems and the internal state management of many functions, especially those involving memory allocation like malloc(). The C standard (ISO/IEC 9899:2011) is quite restrictive, specifying that only a very limited set of functions, primarily abort(), _Exit(), quick_exit(), and signal() itself (with specific arguments), are guaranteed to be safe.
